extracted.intended_audience: news organizations, newsroom leaders, journalists, and media stakeholders interested in the Trust Project Trust Mark and newsroom transparency standards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and announcements about news organizations implementing The Trust Project's 8 Trust Indicators® and earning the Trust Mark; aimed at newsrooms integrating transparency, policies, and training across platforms. Includes research findings and related commitments to fight misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8 Trust Indicators®
rubrics_metrics.description: The core Trust Project standard that news organizations implement to earn the Trust Mark; described as a “gold standard” in journalism transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented across journalistic processes, the news site, podcasts, video and even print; the indicators are built into newsroom workflows to demonstrate transparency and integrity. Organizations referenced worked closely with the Trust Project to incorporate the 8 Trust Indicators®.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust Mark (network membership) / Verified journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Earning the Trust Mark indicates a news organization has implemented the Trust Indicators and joined the Trust Project network, offering "verified journalism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Trust Mark is awarded after organizations incorporate the indicators and work with the Trust Project; membership signals commitment to independent journalism of public value and helps audiences identify trustworthy news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practices: rigorous, clear policies and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of Best Practices defined as rigorous, clear policies and standards with a commitment to back them up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites in the U.S. and Canada went live immediately with their Best Practices after a months-long detailed upgrade; Best Practices serve as an anchor Trust Indicator and require clear institutional policies that are implemented and upheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate opinion and paid content from news
rubrics_metrics.description: A Trust Indicator/content policy requiring clear separation between opinion content, paid content (sponsored content), and news reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit separation is listed among the fundamentals of honest journalism emphasized by the Trust Project; this helps audiences distinguish reporting from advocacy or sponsored material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect newsgathering from funder influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle requiring newsrooms to safeguard newsgathering processes from funders and to disclose any funder relationships that could affect coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as part of the fundamentals the Trust Indicators emphasize; implies policies and practices that prevent funder control over editorial decisions and transparency about funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve the public interest / hold power to account
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should serve the public interest by holding power to account, reporting on solutions to everyday problems, and serving as a platform for the voiceless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as one of the fundamentals of honest journalism and a goal of organizations earning the Trust Mark (e.g., local outlets striving to serve communities and fill news gaps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures including AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust Indicator guidance to include deeper disclosures about the use of AI in journalism and publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page references "deeper disclosures including AI" as part of expansions and upgrades — newsrooms should disclose AI usage practices to audiences as part of transparency efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and integration of Trust Indicators across platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing the standard requires months of training and integration of the Trust Project standard on air and online (and across other delivery formats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful adoption includes staff training and embedding indicators into multiple formats (broadcast, online, podcasts, print) so transparency is visible to audiences regardless of medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic transparency elements improve credibility and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency elements (the Trust Indicators) are read by users and significantly strengthen credibility and trust in news, according to eye-tracking research cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research (University of Georgia DMAC Lab and Trust Project) found that transparency elements are noticed by users and especially benefit news skeptics, demonstrating practical value of visible disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to independent journalism of public value
rubrics_metrics.description: An organizational commitment to independent journalism that serves public value, as a criterion for Trust Project affiliation and the Trust Mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighted across announcements as a defining feature of Trust Project members — commitment must be demonstrable through practices, policies, and newsroom behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in continuous education on misinformation and trusted sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder pledge criterion: invest resources in continuous education of employees, clients and audiences on information threats and trusted media sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ICCO-Trust Project pledge consists of ten commitments focusing on resourcing education about misinformation; news organizations and media stakeholders are expected to devote ongoing resources to this work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize ethics and depth for community trust (Native communities example)
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess trustworthiness among Native news users, newsrooms must prioritize ethics and depth in coverage relevant to those communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings from Trust Project research with Indigenous Media Freedom Alliance indicate Native community members value ethics and depth and are reluctant to trust news lacking those qualities — implying criteria for culturally informed, in-depth reporting.
